summary: We have developed an interactive application for the comparative analysis of this data over time for selected ocean regions. As part of this effort, we developed a system for downloading and standardizing data from the Giovanni portal. We also conducted our own research using this system to identify correlations in data on chlorophyll, light refraction, and temperature in areas with large garbage patches.
details:
Project Overview & How It Works

NASA Earth System Trend Detective is an interactive Earth science discovery platform created for the "Be An Earth System Trend Detective!" challenge. The platform investigates over 23 years of satellite observations (July 2002 - October 2025, spanning 282 monthly timesteps) across all five major subtropical ocean gyres.

Users can explore 2D equirectangular maps and a 3D interactive globe, scrub through multi-decadal timelines, and compare the core plastic accumulation zones against paired North and South background control boundaries. For every selected region and physical variable, including Sea Surface Temperature, Chlorophyll-a, Diffuse Attenuation, Reflectance, Salinity, and Microplastic Radar Proxies. The platform automatically computes 12-month moving averages, Ordinary Least Squares decadal trendlines, spatial contrasts, and statistical significance tests.

Benefits & Scientific Value

Debunking Common Myths with Hard Data: Many assume optical satellites can directly spot floating garbage patches from space. By testing optical anomalies across all five gyres against control zones, our tool proves that 4 km resolution optical sensors do not directly detect dispersed sub-millimeter microplastics.

Uncovering Hidden Climate Signals: While plastic particles remain invisible to optical sensors, our statistical engine reveals a critical planetary trend: subtropical gyres are warming by +0.3C to +0.6C per decade. This thermal stratification blocks nutrient-rich deep water from rising, causing photosynthetic Chlorophyll-a to drop by -6% to -8 per decade in major gyres, turning plastic accumulation zones into rapidly expanding "ocean deserts".


Intended Impact

Our goal is to bridge the gap between raw, complex NASA satellite repositories and accessible public understanding. By pairing rigorous oceanographic metrics with automated, human-readable "Data Detective Case Briefings" the platform empowers students, citizen scientists, educators, and policymakers to move beyond surface-level misconceptions and understand how ocean warming and marine pollution intersect in real time.

Tools, Languages, Software & Hardware

  • Programming Language: Python 3.11
  • Data Acquisition & Processing: NASA earthaccess API, xarray, numpy, pandas and GeoJSON spatial parsing for automated retrieval and normalization of NASA MODIS Aqua, SMAP, and CYGNSS datasets.
  • Frontend & Visualization: Streamlit (interactive web dashboard), PyVista ( 3D globe rendering), and Plotly (interactive multi-region time series and statistical charts).

How Our Project Is Creative

Instead of presenting users with raw charts and expecting them to interpret complex NetCDF files, we framed climate data analysis as an interactive scientific detective investigation. We structured the platform around testing a compelling hypothesis ("Can satellites see the Great Pacific Garbage Patch?"), leading users through a controlled experiment with paired North/South ocean baselines, and culminating in a surprising twist, discovering the expansion of oligotrophic ocean deserts. Automated "Case Briefings" dynamically translate p-values and decadal slopes into clear narrative insights alongside every graph.


Key Factors Our Team Considered

  1. Eliminating False Positives
  2. Statistical Validity in Climate Data
  3. Performance & Responsiveness
  4. Reproducibility
